title: Lithium, anticonvulsant mood stabilisers and antipsychotics: three routes to a calmer mood
ariaLabel: Schematic of three drivers of mania: inositol and GSK-3 signalling inside neurons, excitability through sodium channels, and dopamine signalling. Lithium acts on inositol and GSK-3 signalling, valproate and carbamazepine reduce sodium channel excitability, and antipsychotics block dopamine D2 receptors.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or lipid value is shown or implied.
blockInfo: A drug of the chosen class acting at this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape). Less passes here, with the effects shown at the cholesterol and the LDL receptors.

nodes.label: Inositol and GSK-3
nodes.info: Intracellular signalling that lithium is thought to damp.

nodes.label: Sodium channel firing
nodes.info: Rapid firing through voltage-gated sodium channels.

nodes.label: Neuron excitability
nodes.info: Excitability that contributes to a manic episode.

nodes.label: Dopamine signal
nodes.info: Dopamine signalling in the limbic system.

nodes.label: Manic symptoms
nodes.info: A teaching score for the intensity of manic symptoms.

edges.label: IMPase and GSK-3
edges.info: Lithium inhibits inositol monophosphatase and glycogen synthase kinase 3, which lowers over-active second messenger signalling. This is the leading explanation; the full mechanism is not settled.
Adds to the effect shown at the right.

edges.label: sodium channels
edges.info: Valproate and carbamazepine block voltage-gated sodium channels in rapidly firing neurons (valproate also raises GABA).
Adds to the effect shown at the right.

edges.label: D2 receptors
edges.info: Antipsychotics block dopamine D2 receptors (second-generation drugs also block 5-HT2A receptors), which lowers agitation and psychotic symptoms.
Adds to the effect shown at the right.

sources: Where each class acts. Lithium acts on inositol and GSK-3 signalling, valproate and carbamazepine reduce sodium channel firing, and antipsychotics block dopamine D2 receptors. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Lamotrigine for bipolar depression, antidepressants, levels and toxicity of lithium (narrow range, kidney and thyroid effects), pregnancy risks, interactions, long-term maintenance and adverse effects are left out. Manic symptoms are drawn as a teaching score. Levels and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
